title: The Nichiren schools
hook: many schools follow Nichiren's focus on the Lotus Sutra's title

segments.voice: Yesterday, the letter A, the Shingon sound set at the start of everything. Your line was ah. Did it turn up anywhere, in a sigh or a laugh? Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

A low, steady sound comes through an apartment door, the same words over and over, like a train on a long track. Nam myoho renge kyo. Inside, a few neighbors sit side by side, hands pressed together, facing a small wooden cabinet. It sounds like a mantra, and in a way it works like one. But it is something more surprising: it is a title. It is the name of a book, said out loud, with a word of devotion in front of it. A whole family of Buddhist schools grew up around saying that name. Today: the Nichiren schools.
screen: `A SOUND THROUGH A DOOR.` → `NAM MYOHO RENGE KYO.` → `IT IS A TITLE.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Nichiren was a Japanese monk who trained in the Tendai school, the one we met a few days ago, where the Lotus Sutra was already held in honor. Tradition says he studied widely and came away convinced that the Lotus Sutra was the heart of the Buddha's teaching, and that his country needed to turn back to it. He said so loudly, and in the stories his followers tell, he paid for it with exile and danger. Second, the big idea. Nichiren taught that the title of the Lotus Sutra is not just a label on the cover. It holds the whole sutra inside it, the way a seed holds a tree, or a name holds a person. So saying the title with faith is a way of taking in the entire teaching at once. The practice is called daimoku, which means the title. Third, the words themselves. Myoho renge kyo is the Japanese reading of the sutra's name: the wonderful dharma, the lotus flower, the sutra. In front goes namu, or nam, a word of devotion, something like I give myself to. In Sanskrit the sutra is called the Saddharma Pundarika, the lotus of the true dharma. Some communities chant nam myoho renge kyo, others namu myoho renge kyo. Same title, a different breath. Fourth, what came after. Nichiren left disciples, and they and their students built many schools and lineages. Some are temple traditions with priests. Some are lay movements that meet in living rooms. They share the sutra and the chant, and they disagree, sometimes sharply, about other things, which we will come to in the next few days. What they hold in common is this: a few words, said out loud and meant, can open the Buddha's teaching right in the middle of an ordinary life, at a kitchen table, before work, in a small apartment with the neighbors.
screen: `A MONK NAMED NICHIREN.` · `THE TITLE HOLDS THE WHOLE SUTRA.` · `NAM MYOHO RENGE KYO.` · `MANY SCHOOLS, ONE TITLE.` · then, large: `THE TITLE.`

segments.voice: Here is how people do it, if you'd like to try. Sit upright. Bring your palms together in front of your chest. In Nichiren practice people face a scroll; you can face a wall or a window. Say the title once, slowly and clearly: nam myoho renge kyo. Then let the sound fade and sit in the quiet it leaves. If the words are not yours to say, hear them once in your mind instead, as a name a whole community holds dear. Notice where in your body the sound landed. Stay with that place. The bell holds the time.
The Nichiren schools. The Buddhist communities that follow the Japanese monk Nichiren in honoring the Lotus Sutra and chanting its title. Today's word.
Your line: the title. Today, notice one name you say without thinking, a street, a song, a friend, and say it once on purpose, as if it held the whole thing. Day one thousand three hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Nichiren Buddhists chant the title of the Lotus Sutra, nam myoho renge kyo (or namu myoho renge kyo), often with palms together before a scroll, alone or together in temples and homes.

fork.setup: you're Nichiren. the people who come to you have little time to study a long sutra. what do you give them?
options: a short summary of every chapter.
the sutra's title, to say out loud.
a rule to read nothing but the sutra.
fork.reveal: he gives them the title. in his teaching, the title holds the whole sutra, so anyone can take it in by chanting it.

original.note: Sanskrit Saddharma Pundarika, the lotus of the true dharma: the Lotus Sutra, whose Japanese title is myoho renge kyo.

trapdoor: what you thought: nam myoho renge kyo is a magic phrase.
what it means: it is the Lotus Sutra's title with a word of devotion in front, chanted because Nichiren taught that the title holds the whole sutra.
what a scholar hears: daimoku, the title, set at the center of practice by a monk who trained in Tendai, where the Lotus Sutra was already honored.

notes: Gloss of namu as a word of devotion ('I give myself to') and of myoho renge kyo as 'the wonderful dharma, the lotus flower, the sutra': confirm wording acceptable across Nichiren communities.
Nam vs namu: Soka Gakkai and Nichiren Shoshu typically say nam, Nichiren Shu typically namu; script says only 'some communities', confirm.
Exile and danger in Nichiren's life is given as what his followers tell; confirm framing.
Practice invites the listener to say the title once; confirm a Keeper is comfortable with a non-member saying it.
Hook scene (neighbors before a wooden cabinet, i.e. butsudan) is an illustration, not a specific community.
Editor: fork setup no longer asserts that Nichiren's hearers were farmers and workers who would never read a sutra (unsourced claim); now 'little time to study a long sutra'.
